t: #3550 Smallest Index With Digit Sum Equal to Index
o: Scan indices left to right; for each nums[i], compute the sum of its decimal digits and return i the first time it equals i. Values are ≤ 1000 so digit sums are at most 27, while indices can exceed that — many arrays will return -1. Examples: [1,3,2] → 2; [1,10,11] → 1 (smallest match wins); [1,2,3] → -1. With n ≤ 100, any direct scan works.
k: Digit sum of a number ≤ 1000 is at most 27, so large indices rarely match.
A single left-to-right scan returns the smallest valid index naturally.

a.n: Approach 1: Linear Scan with Digit Sum
a.i: For each index, extract digits arithmetically (or via string conversion) and compare the sum to the index; return on the first match.
s: Compute digitSum(nums[i]) by repeated division by 10.
If digitSum == i, return i; after the loop return -1.
a.t: O(n log(max nums)) — each number has O(digits) extraction.

a.i: Convert each number to a string and sum its character digits — equally valid and arguably clearer for small inputs.
s: Sum the numeric values of the characters of str(nums[i]).
Return i on the first equality, else -1.
a.t: O(n · digits) — same asymptotics with string overhead.

w: Trivial problem — just don't forget the -1 case and note nums[i] can be 0 (digit sum 0, matches index 0). Follow-ups: largest such index, count of matches, or digit-product variant.
